content.title: Ruling on Participating in and Giving Greetings on Non-Muslim Religious Festivals
content.subtitle: May the lights of celebration not blur the boundaries of Tawheed.
content.body:
During the autumn days, the monotonous beat of drums and the noise drifting from afar, along with the artificial lights and lively commotion around the mandaps, create a strange atmosphere. Many consider it harmless to visit out of mere curiosity at a friend’s request or to admire the decorations of clay idols. We may think, “I am not offering anjali, nor am I raising my hands in worship or devotion; I have only come to look!” But have we ever stopped to think—when the sovereignty of the very Lord before whom we prostrate at least seventeen times every day in our obligatory prayers and say, “You alone we worship,” is denied, and His own creation is placed on the seat of worship and prayed to, how great an act of self-deception and spiritual heedlessness can a believer’s mere presence there out of curiosity become?

The Call of Monotheism and Divine Injunction

Allah, the Lord of the worlds, has declared unequivocally in the Holy Quran:

“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him…” (Surah An-Nisa, 4:36)

The greatest asset in a believer’s life is Iman—unwavering conviction in Tawheed. The clay idol before which heads are bowed, and which is presumed to be a source of provision or power, is not part of a mere folk exhibition. It is a direct ceremonial ritual that sets up rivals beside the One Creator of the universe.

Silent Validation Behind ‘Shubho Sharadiya

Many assume that uttering courteous words to please a friend causes no harm. Yet, the premise of Durga Puja revolves around the invocation and veneration of a deity. When a Muslim offers greetings like “Shubho Sharadiya” or “Shubho Bijoya,” they inadvertently extend inner affirmation toward that very polytheistic ritual. Can a true believer ever proclaim: “May your act of Shirk be blessed,” or “May worshiping other than Allah bring good fortune?” Allah has designated Shirk as the supreme injustice, declaring that while He forgives other sins, He will not forgive associating partners with Him (Surah An-Nisa, 4:48). Entering such spaces under the guise of curiosity deeply compromises a believer's spiritual dignity.

Festive Pandals: Zones of Divine Disapproval

Amidst burning incense and ringing bells, we might stand purely as detached onlookers without performing rituals. Nevertheless, our physical presence swells the crowd, lending festive grandeur to a public display of Shirk. Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) issued a cautionary counsel:

“Do not enter upon the polytheists in their places of worship on the day of their festival, for divine wrath descends upon them.” (As-Sunan al-Kubra: 18862)

Where divine displeasure descends, no believer’s heart can discover wholesome joy or permissible recreation.

Compassionate Conduct versus the Line of Faith

Does this mean treating non-Muslims harshly or abandoning them in hardship? Absolutely not. Islam strictly forbids injustice toward people of other faiths and prohibits insulting their deities (Surah Al-An‘am, 6:108). Safeguarding their rights, visiting them during illness, and showing neighborly compassion are binding duties upon every Muslim. However, social benevolence and theological compromise are never the same. Showing fairness to a non-Muslim neighbor never requires dismantling the boundaries of faith.

Let not the fleeting glitter of festive lights dim the inner radiance of La ilaha illallah. A heart rooted in monotheism cannot stand willingly before an altar where the Sovereign Lord is denied for a clay idol. Let us preserve mutual compassion while guarding our Tawheed with deep devotion.
